system: You are a helpful assistant. Make sure your answer addresses every request in the message.
message:
I run deliveries for a small furniture restorer and I've got a few things to sort for tomorrow.

Can you suggest a name for our new delivery van (staff vote, nothing rude)?

Tomorrow the van can't leave the depot before 08:30 and must be back by 12:00. Three drops, each takes 15 minutes to unload. Drop A has a delivery window of 09:00 to 10:00. Drop B is a shop that needs its delivery done before it opens at 09:30. Drop C is an office that won't accept anything before 11:00. Driving times: depot to A 30 min, depot to B 20 min, depot to C 45 min, A to B 25 min, A to C 40 min, B to C 50 min. The driver also needs a 30-minute break somewhere before 12:00. What order should he go in, and what's the timeline?

Could you also rewrite our delivery text so it sounds friendlier than "Driver arriving. Be in."? List three things the driver should check on furniture before handing it over. Should we give customers a paper delivery note or an emailed one? And define "proof of delivery" in a line for our new part-timer. One more thing: we're thinking of texting customers the evening before with a rough arrival time. Could you draft that evening-before text too, keeping it under 160 characters so it goes as a single message?
response:
# Delivery plan for tomorrow

## Van name (for the staff vote)
- **Sofa So Good** (my pick)
- **Dovetail**, after the woodworking joint
- **Chester**, after the Chesterfield sofa
- **Van Gogh**
- **The Mover & Shaker**

## Route order: B → A → C
Going to A first doesn't work. You'd reach A at 09:00 and finish at 09:15, then arrive at B at 09:40, after it opens. B has to go first.

| Time | Activity |
|---|---|
| 08:30 | Leave depot |
| 08:50 | Arrive at B and unload (20 min drive) |
| 09:05 | Finish at B, 25 min before it opens |
| 09:30 | Arrive at A (25 min drive) and unload, inside the 09:00-10:00 window |
| 09:45 | Finish at A and leave |
| 10:25 | Arrive near C (40 min drive) and park up |
| 10:25-10:55 | 30-minute driver break |
| 11:00 | Start unloading at C, the earliest it will accept |
| 11:15 | Finish at C and leave |
| 12:00 | Back at depot (45 min drive) |

**There is no buffer at the end.** C can't start before 11:00, and the drive back takes 45 minutes after a 15-minute unload, so the van returns at exactly 12:00. A late start or a slow unload at C will make him late back. The only slack is the 10:25-11:00 gap, which the break uses. If you want some safety margin, ask whether C could take delivery slightly earlier or whether the 12:00 return can move.

## Friendlier delivery text
> Hi [Name], your [Shop] delivery is on its way! [Driver] will be with you around [time]. Please make sure someone is there to receive it. See you soon!

## Three checks before handover
1. **Surface and finish:** look for new scratches, chips, cracks or marks, and compare against the restoration photos.
2. **Stability and moving parts:** check that joints are solid, legs don't wobble, and drawers and doors open and close properly.
3. **Completeness:** confirm all parts, hardware (handles, keys, shelves) and the item itself match the order, and that it's clean and dry.

## Paper or emailed delivery note?
I'd go with **emailed** as the default, ideally with a signature or photo taken on the driver's phone. It can't be lost, is easy to search if there's a dispute, costs nothing, and can include condition photos. Keep a paper copy as a fallback for customers without email or who prefer it.

## Proof of delivery
**Proof of delivery (POD)** is a record, usually a signature, photo or timestamped note, showing that the goods arrived in good condition and were received by the customer.

## Evening-before text (about 134 characters with placeholders)
> Hi [Name], [Shop] here. Your delivery is due tomorrow, roughly [time]. We'll text when the driver's close. Need to change? Just reply.

That leaves about 26 characters of room once the placeholders are filled in. Keep your shop name short, and use plain straight apostrophes rather than curly ones, because special characters can force the message to split into two texts.
